description: I am just here for the experience!
summary: Our Neighbor’s Map is a free web app that helps the first astronauts on Mars plan a safe Marswalk or rover drive and do science along the way. It layers data from seven NASA missions (Viking, Mars Global Surveyor, Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Curiosity, Perseverance and NASA’s space-weather service), plus ESA Mars Express, into one map of the whole planet. Pick a base, add science stops, and it finds a route around steep slopes, crater walls and loose sand. It then gives a safety score that explains itself in plain words: oxygen and suit battery use, walk-back distance, daylight, radio contact with the habitat, radiation and live solar storms. Crews can replay the walk, fly it in 3D, measure distances, and explore high-value survey sites such as ancient river valleys, buried ice and a proposed ocean shoreline. Mars Trek shows the planet; our tool decides whether a specific walk is safe and why. That turns decades of orbital data into the hyperlocal, safety-first plan an astronaut needs.
details:
What it does: A layered, interactive map of all of Mars with a step-by-step EVA and rover planner. Simple mode guides beginners in three steps (Explore Mars → Plan a walk or drive → Is it safe?). Technical mode shows every layer, number and setting.

How it works:

  • Terrain: MOLA elevation tiles, with HRSC/MOLA 200 m shaded relief for local steepness, crater walls and scarps.
    • Sun and daylight from NASA GISS Mars24.
    • Radiation from the Curiosity RAD surface baseline.
    • Live solar storms from NASA DONKI, Curiosity weather (REMS) and the latest Perseverance photos.
  • Radio: line-of-sight from the habitat mast over terrain and the curve of Mars.
  • Safety score: each hazard becomes a survival factor, multiplied together, with plain-English reasons. Missing data counts as unknown, never as safe.
  • Water & ice layers: ancient valley networks (Hynek et al. 2010), ice-exposing impacts (Dundas et al. 2014) and glacier-like forms (Souness et al. 2012), plus the proposed Deuteronilus ocean level (Head et al. 1999), computed from MOLA.
  • Real-detail zoom: HiRISE 25 cm photos where they exist. Elsewhere, zoom stops at the sharpest real photo, because we never invent terrain.

Benefits and impact: It turns scattered orbital datasets into one decision: is this walk safe, and why? It helps mission planners, analog-mission crews, students and the public understand what keeps astronauts alive on Mars.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Leaflet for maps; Three.js for 3D; Python for an optional local server; Playwright for automated testing (300+ tests); GitHub Pages and Actions for hosting. The NASA API key is stored as a GitHub secret. It runs in any browser with no install and works on phones.

Creativity: It’s a decision tool, not just a viewer, with a safety score that shows its reasoning. It adds radio line-of-sight blackouts, a 3D fly-through and Simple/Technical modes.

Factors considered:

  • Astronaut safety first.
  • Suit mobility and carried gear.
  • Honest data limits. Boulders smaller than the terrain grid are flagged for HiRISE checks; 1 m terrain models are on the roadmap.
  • Stale feeds are labelled.
  • Accessibility, phone use and security: shared plan links are validated.

SI use: Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code, debugging, testing, documentation and editing the demo video. This is also disclosed in the README and page metadata.
